articles.title: Black holes keep tearing these stars apart, but they survive
articles.description: Astronomers have found stars that repeatedly skim past supermassive black holes, surviving each encounter while producing a new burst of light. In some systems, those flares mysteriously fade with every return. Researchers now think the key may be stars that were already spinning extremely fast before being captured. That rapid rotation could explain both the fading flares and how the stars ended up in such extraordinarily tight black hole orbits.

articles.title: Baltimore transit 101: a guide to going carless in Charm City
articles.description: As an incoming freshman at Hopkins, you'll receive many welcomes to Baltimore, the city you can now call home. You'll receive advice on how to engage and interact with the city as part of your freshman programming, yet it often overlooks a key aspect of participating in daily life in Baltimore: how to get around. If you're anything like me, a New Yorker who never had to learn how to drive, coming to Baltimore may feel like a big change for you. It's no secret that Baltimore's transit options somewhat lag behind other Northeastern cities. However, with a little bit of knowledge and patience, you'll be able to get yourself around the Baltimore area like an expert. Honorable mention: JHMI and Blue Jay Shuttles Most likely, this will be the first form of transportation that you'll be exposed to during your orientation. The Johns Hopkins Medical Institute (JHMI) shuttle runs from Homewood Campus to the Hopkins Hospital while stopping by important landmarks such as the Peabody Institute, Penn Station and the JHU-MICA Film Center. This bus route is run by the University and is free for students, making it an excellent and reliable way to commute, especially if you work on the med campus or are a Peabody student. My favorite part about using the JHMI shuttle is that it's much easier to know when your bus is coming compared to city buses, since you can track their location on the TransLoc app. Speaking of the TransLoc app, from 6:00 p.m. to 2:00 a.m., you can request a Blue Jay Shuttle, which functions as the University's rideshare service, for free. If you are within the zone indicated on TransLoc, you'll be able to request a free ride to anywhere else within the zone. If the University-owned shuttle doesn't come within fifteen minutes, the University will send a Lyft free of charge instead--in my experience, the shuttles are often running late, so you'll be sent the Lyft more often than not. Still, no matter how long it takes, it beats paying for an Uber any day. Method 1: City buses Since there is no direct rail access to Homewood Campus, you'll most likely be relying on city buses when taking public transit. When taking the buses in Baltimore, you need to be aware that there are two distinct bus services: the Maryland Transit Administration (MTA) BaltimoreLink and the Charm City Circulator. The BaltimoreLink is run by the MTA, owned by the Maryland state government, and is a public expansive service throughout the entire Baltimore area, whereas the Charm City Circulator is run by Baltimore's municipal government, and its service area is more limited . However, the Charm City Circulator is free of charge, while the MTA's buses cost two dollars per ride as of 2026. You can catch the Charm City Circulator Purple Route on 33rd Street, just outside of the Kajiken restaurant, across from the campus bookstore. The Purple Route runs in a clockwise loop and can take you to the Waverly neighborhood, Penn Station and Inner Harbor. You can catch the MTA's CityLink Silver bus line on the corner of Saint Paul Street and 31st Street, which will take you directly down Saint Paul Street to Penn Station, Inner Harbor and the Federal Hill neighborhood, which is not covered by the Circulator's Purple Route. Note that, unlike the Circulator which only runs in one direction, the CityLink Silver runs along different streets depending on if the bus is northbound or southbound. The southbound service runs on Saint Paul Street while the northbound service runs on Charles Street. Method 2: Subway and light rail Baltimore isn't completely devoid of rail transit - many Baltimoreans rely on the city's subway system and light rail network to commute. The Baltimore Light RailLink is a light rail system (a smaller, more condensed subway system that often runs on the street) that carries users to Hunt Valley, Glen Burnie, north Baltimore City or the Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (Pro tip: taking the light rail to the airport is much easier and cheaper than taking an Uber or a commuter train). However, the closest stop to Homewood Campus is the North Avenue station, which is over a mile away, so it isn't the best option for most Hopkins students. For Peabody students, the light rail is much more convenient, since the Mount Vernon station on the light rail is very close to Peabody. I have only needed to use the light rail once, when I needed to get from the convention center in the Inner Harbor to Hampden. Even so, from my experience, it was a pleasant ride, and the train came on time. The Baltimore Metro SubwayLink is the city's sole subway route, running underground through most of downtown Baltimore. The line's terminus is at the Hopkins Hospital, which is convenient for those who frequent the Medical Campus; however, it runs even further away from Homewood campus. Unfortunately, I have never had the pleasure of using it, though I hope to in the future. Method 3: Commuter rail and Washington Metro With Washington D.C. only around 40 miles away from Baltimore, you would be remiss not to check out our nation's capital as you're getting adjusted to campus life. The Maryland Area Regional Commuter (MARC) Train is the Baltimore-Washington area's commuter rail system. You can catch the MARC train from Baltimore's Penn Station, which is easily accessed by Baltimore's transit (or the JHMI), and ride the MARC train for about an hour to get to Washington D.C. Union Station, the last stop on the line. From there, you can transfer to the Washington Metro, which is a very reliable way to get around the city. At Union Station, you can transfer to the Red Line which can take you to attractions such as the White House and the National Mall. Overall, Baltimore is not as daunting as it seems to get around by public transit. Whether you're like me and refuse to get your license, or if you have to navigate life without a car for the first time ever, the city's public transit options are always available, even if they're not the most punctual. Getting outside of the 'Hopkins bubble' is very important for your enjoyment of the city. Whether you want to visit the National Aquarium, check out restaurants in Federal Hill or see our nation's capital, know you don't always have to get behind the wheel to do it. Henry Serringer is a sophomore majoring in Writing Seminars from New York, N.Y. He is a News and Features Editor for The News-Letter .

articles.title: Fells Point: an immigration story
articles.description: In March 2026, a Baltimore furniture dealer signed a $25 million contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The contract stated that the deal represented "support of the administration's immigration and enforcement priorities," in addition to the material agreement of supplying furniture for ICE offices. The deal inspired outrage throughout Baltimore, especially in Fells Point. F ells Point, a historical port city, was settled by William Fell in the early 18th century and given its grid design by Fell's son, Edward. The neighborhood served as a major hub of movement in America during the 19th and 20th centuries, attracting European immigrants, most often Irish and German , as well as African American migrants . Between the mid-18th century and the mid-20th century, over 2 million immigrants landed in Baltimore. Fells Point was the second-leading point of entry after only New York City's Ellis Island. There is evidence of correspondence, such as a letter in which a sister who has arrived at Ellis Island seeks her brother , between the port cities. Fells Point was able to attract people with its abundance of housing and job opportunities. The Baltimore and Ohio (B&O) Railroad created geographical connections that improved travel and created jobs in construction for immigrants in Fells Point. Once settling in Fells Point, immigrants frequently inhabited row houses. In 1868, the B&O Railroad opened the first immigration pier, Locust Point, beginning the shift of immigration away from Fells Point . The celebration of the new pier, including a parade, was held in Fells Point . Then, when Fells Point was unable to accommodate the 20th-century transition to steamships, it lost its position as Baltimore's main port. In the early 20th century, majority-Black streets were demolished as part of "slum-clearance" to make room for White immigrant families. In the late 20th century, Fells Point developed a reputation as an unsafe neighborhood, with high crime rates. Fells Point became Maryland's first historic district in 1969 and though it continues to stand as an ethnically and culturally diverse neighborhood in Baltimore, it has become increasingly occupied by White homeowners (making up 70% of residents). However, critics claim that the gentrification of Fells Point has eliminated "third places," public and free-to-use spaces like parks and libraries, and pushed the working class out of the neighborhood. The neighborhood now has a lower-than-national-average age and higher-than-national-average household income. The shift in national attitudes toward immigration began well before the private furniture store's deal in 2026. In 2007, the Department of Homeland Security raided Fells Point, detaining approximately 30 immigrants. In 2018, Fells Point was one of many American cities that participated in Love Knows No Borders, holding a vigil for asylum seekers and citing the neighborhood's immigrant history as one of many reasons to protect its neighbors. Yet, less than a decade later, in July 2026, ICE officers arrested parents at Commodore John Rodgers , a school just north of Fells Point. Private security and the Baltimore Police Department (BPD) presence are also expected to be increased in Fells Point this summer. Although the BPD cannot work directly with ICE and Governor Moore spoke firmly against ICE actions that inspire terror, he has promised that Baltimore's collaboration with federal agencies will continue when he deems it necessary to ensure safety. Fells Point is one of few neighborhoods in Baltimore, outside of the "Hopkins Bubble," that Hopkins students consistently visit. Let this be a nudge to new Blue Jays, as you all now become Baltimore community members, to take a moment to notice historical markers, police presence, emerging infrastructure, closed restaurants and our fellow neighbors when they venture to Fells point - or anywhere else in Baltimore city. Honora Muratori is a sophomore majoring in History and Political Science from New York City, N.Y. She is a News & Features Editor for The News-Letter.

articles.title: Making Homewood campus your home
articles.description: No matter the environment you originally call home, welcome to Hopkins! You'll soon make your transition from the comfort of your own home to the bustling atmosphere of Charles Village and the Homewood campus. Here are a few (hopefully) helpful points about making campus your new home, coming from someone who was completely unfamiliar with Baltimore before freshman year. At the heart of settling into your new environment is being familiar with that environment itself. Strolling around while on the phone with a family member back home, walking into different buildings and finding restrooms, charting your path to class during orientation week - these are all things you can do to not only get outside but also familiarize yourself with campus spaces. Familiarity goes hand in hand with comfort. During orientation week, your First-Year Mentors will help guide you around campus too. I recommend checking out Bloomberg Hall, Gilman Hall and "The Stuce," our new student center. For food on campus, it's best that you try out every dining hall as soon as possible. Personally, I believe that Hopkins Café serves the best food because it has tried-and-true stations like the sandwich bar. Nolan's on 33rd is great for its build-your-own-bowls and, in my opinion, pudding cups and cookies. Levering Kitchens is a food-court style hall with different food stalls, and it is a great place to have a meal in between study sessions due to its proximity to Brody and Gilman Hall. Speaking of, you should also get comfortable with some study spots... you'll need them. There are the classics, such as the Brody Reading Room and the MSE Library Annex, which are great for finals season or Tuesday night homework sessions, but I also suggest finding some rather uncommon places. This is great not only to change your environment, which you may find helps with productivity, but also to take advantage of all the areas that Hopkins provides for its students. You can check out an empty seminar-style classroom in Gilman Hall, the upstairs floor of Bloomberg or even the tables in Malone Hall. A personal favorite of mine is finding an empty classroom and setting up shop for the duration of my studying. In terms of the social scene, while Hopkins is not known for being the most lively, rah-rah environment, there are more than enough outlets for an actual social life. Greek life is a path many, such as myself, take, but it is certainly not the only way to find a community. It's extremely important that you make an effort to meet people and join different groups, especially during the first few months of freshman year. This is how friend groups form and commitments begin. If research is your strong suit, reach out to professors and labs to see if they'll take you on early. For those of you who go to the gym, create a schedule, stick to it and try your best to do so even when course loads ramp up. These are rather general suggestions that I've been describing above and can (relatively) be said about pretty much any campus. So, I'll provide some of my own advice on how to live on the Homewood campus and want to call it your home. First, immediately try to leave your dorm at the beginning of your first semester - the freshman dorms aren't the best environment, anyway. Go outside, do work in different places and hang out with some people you've met during orientation week. Hopkins can feel isolating at times with such a competitive environment, especially if you're pre-med, but once you find places you are comfortable in with other students who you enjoy being around, the grind is a lot more friendly. Second, find a routine with your meals. This seems obvious, but once midterms begin on their usual schedule and courses and extracurriculars become more demanding, you should be steady with your meal times. After the first few weeks of classes, regiment a meal routine - bonus points if it's at different dining halls. Third, meet as many people as you can, truly. In making campus your home, it's crucial that you hope to find a community that you can ride with for your time on Homewood. Shaan Udani is a junior majoring in Public Health Studies from Morris Plains, N.J. He is a Science and Technology Editor for The News-Letter.

articles.title: A call away
articles.description: Sunday evening: sitting at one end of the Undergraduate Teaching Labs with a cold box of Hopkins Cafe food, adjacent to an empty chem lab... the space felt too quiet and strangely empty. I adjusted my AirPods, thumb hovering over the call log info button with my mom. 43 minutes. Six more than the day before. Yet it wasn't just the yearning of a warm embrace, familiar voice or home cooked meal I found myself yearning for. It was simply home. Upon my curious search of "define home," Google instead automatically outputted "define homeostasis." Oddly enough, that felt like the more fitting option. "Home" is difficult to define when it is more than the physical. While "What is your hometown?" can be a straightforward answer, "What is home for you?" draws a plethora of others like belonging, vision, community, love, security or sanctuary. The unexpected suggestion of "homeostasis" made me realize how much internal stability built through familiarity grounded me in times of homesickness, especially the things I could control and surround myself with, like watching sunsets, attending Bible studies, immersing myself in a solid read or shooting hoops. I realized the interests, and especially, routines I had established in New York, could be continued in Baltimore, comforting me as if not everything had changed. Breaking larger tasks into smaller, approachable wins brought a sense of satisfying consistency and familiarity, alleviating both my mind and heart. To this end, I learned the difference between comforting myself and distracting myself. Calling my mom helped. Subconsciously pushing those feelings deeper and replacing them for temporary adrenaline rushes didn't. Neither did romanticizing home, my head space stubbornly stuck in New York, contemplating the things I could and should be doing. Sometimes hanging up calls felt like blowing out a dying candlelight. But this cycle of expectation and unhealthy idealization only deepened my homesickness because when the phrase "There's no place like home" became my measuring stick, I wasn't just missing home. I was waiting for college to end so I could return to it. Homesickness thus called me to be honest with my feelings and the ways I could face it proactively rather than suppress. I am still working on being more present and open-minded on campus, to find gratitude in the learning and exploring that comes from moving away. What had personally made homesickness even harder was seeing those around me adjust so smoothly. The ways they were exploring and embracing Baltimore, constantly out with friends while staying on top of their schedules and seemingly piling more commitments by the week brought shame to my internal distractions. Then, one afternoon shuttling back from Baltimore Penn, I remember noticing a fellow student, suitcase in hand, visibly sighing before stepping off towards the steps of Commons. Maybe they were exhausted from traveling. Maybe they were dreading the incoming workload post spring break. Or maybe they, too, were leaving the home they loved. Homesickness isn't rare. It is often just not openly shared. Moving away from home, to me, used to be a period at the end of a sentence with an indented next paragraph: a clean, abrupt break, leaving the writer grasping for some suitable next word. Reflecting now, I see it as an ellipsis. It was never about diminishing or replacing a home full of what I had already created and experienced for another. It was about having the courage to let home expand. A blinking last dot of the ellipsis waiting patiently for me to move at my own pace to discover home-building as my own architect. My end of first year was repeatedly met with the question "How was it?" Surprisingly, my answer often landed on "I haven't gotten to explore Baltimore as much as I would like to." This underlying reflection that Baltimore has the potential to B-more in my life proves a new seed planted. I am reminded that homesickness eases and resilience is built. I still call home often, and whether they last 43 minutes or not, I am now comfortable being the one to say, "Got to go, bye mom." Katie Park is a sophomore majoring in Molecular and Cellular Biology from Poughkeepsie, N.Y. She is a Sports Editor for The News-Letter .

articles.title: Computer models pinpoint catalysts for replacing fossil-fueled ammonia production
articles.description: Ammonia is one of the most important chemicals produced in the world, ranking second only to sulfuric acid in the total volume produced each year. It is used mostly to make fertilizer, which is essential to feeding the world's population. Yet its production accounts for up to 2% of the world's energy consumption and about 1.5% of greenhouse gas emissions, so the search has been underway for ways to produce ammonia more sustainably.

articles.title: Not sure where you belong yet? Here's a few places to start looking
articles.description: As a freshman, there seems to be endless things to look for: your dorm key, where your classes are, the best coffee order on the Brody menu and the answers for that weekly assignment. To have "found" something often implies that you were once aware of its absence, or were in need of it to the point where you were searching for something that you felt empty without. But what does it mean to find your "place" among thousands of new students and hundreds of new opportunities in a new chapter of life? Being a senior myself, I feel like it wouldn't be my last Cover Letter without imparting some kind of advice to readers from the incoming class. So if you're ever feeling like you have yet to find your place at Hopkins, here's a list of some places to look: In the class you registered for since you didn't get into your first choice By now, you may know it all too well already: waking up suspiciously early to log onto SIS and enter the battlefield to register for your classes in the hopes of crafting the perfect ideal schedule. Yet, there will be some times where you end up getting your second or third choice class, whether it's because of prerequisite requirements, low class seat availability or just plain internet bandwidth issues (one semester, a friend of mine walked from McCoy to Gilman for better Wi-Fi chances). Although the initial disappointment is understandable, you might find that your second choice class was more interesting than you thought. Putting yourself in new and maybe unexpected environments will help you find your people during the beginnings of your first year. You might learn that you're interested in things that you might not even know existed before college. And if you aren't, that's still some useful information to use going forward. Regardless, it's helpful to think of setbacks as opportunities to calibrate your college path, and who knows; you might discover something interesting during the process. Student Involvement Fair (SIF) If you're not sure what you're looking to do in your spare time at Hopkins, SIF will have something to catch your eye. Whether it's crocheting or debate, if you can think of a hobby, there's probably a club for it. Hundreds of student associations gather for SIF and try to recruit new members (us included), so it's definitely a place to look if you're feeling up for wandering around booths. I joined The News-Letter after hearing about it at SIF, and I had my eye on it since I was interested in doing something related to publishing and journalism. It was one of the best decisions I made in college, and I've met so many brilliant and passionate people through the paper. Many of these clubs are looking for freshmen as well, as recruiting new members keeps the club alive and keeps the student body interested in what they have to offer. Even if you have the slightest impulse about the club, there's no harm in going to one general body meeting or event! If anything, you'll meet some new people. If nothing else, the mere act of walking through countless lines of people through deafening noise and club members making slightly uncomfortable eye contact with you perhaps builds character itself. There's bound to be something for everyone, so make sure not to miss this opportunity! On a new walking route back to your dorm Figuring out where things are on campus was one of the most nerve-wracking things for me in my freshman year. My high school was a small one, both in physical size and class size. I could walk around the entire square-shaped campus in less than five minutes if I really wanted to; so despite Hopkins having a medium-sized campus, it was still a pretty noticeable change for me. Being the type of person that needs to know the exact parking situation before driving to meet my friends, remembering where the buildings and entrances were at Hopkins and how to get to my classes was a whole ordeal. But once I figured out where certain walkways connected and where all the shortcuts were, finding my way around campus didn't feel as daunting as it first seemed. Sometimes, a different angle or a change of pace is what you might need in order to find what you're looking for. Using a different walking route may end up in you noticing things you haven't noticed before, like a new cafe to try or an interesting building you might look up online later. Plus, it's a relatively easy thing to do once you're somewhat familiar with the campus layout. Intentionally breaking your routine can help you feel less confined by things that may seem difficult or overwhelming, and put things into perspective. Although the detour may take longer than your preferred route, the possibility of finding something new makes it worth the extra time. The Gatehouse There is a small building nestled right next to one of the side entrances of campus near the Baltimore Museum of Art, with stone walls and a sloping roof that is often covered with branches and other debris. If you look closely, there is actually a sign near the roof that reads, "NEWS LETTER OFFICE." On some late nights, the lights will be on, and you might find yourself wondering what's going on in there. As the home of The News-Letter , the Gatehouse is where all our staff editors gather to have meetings, work on our print editions or just hang out in our spare time. As a staff member myself, it seems only fitting to promote the paper in my magazine piece here. There are so many different sections within the paper that there's bound to be something for everyone, whether that's as a guest writer or a reader. So when you're passing by that side of campus and see the quaint little building, I promise you that it has a purpose (and a great one at that). The printed newspapers lying around campus every few weeks are direct products of our staff's efforts, and your writing could even be featured in it. We are always looking for new writers, and almost any idea of yours can be turned into a great piece. Putting your unique individual perspective into words and out into the world is one of the most important parts of the college experience, and the Gatehouse is where all those stories begin to be delivered to the Hopkins community. How to know when you've "found" it? With all these places that I've recommended where you might find your place at Hopkins, it may still be difficult to know when exactly you've "found it." In reality, your role at Hopkins may not necessarily be something you can touch or actually carry around, so knowing when you've come across it can be hard. Personally, I believe that your "place" is not something that is inherently stationary or static, but rather, something that changes the shape of your character and helps you move toward your greater goals in life. Whether you know what that dream is or you're still figuring it out, the "place" that is meant for you at Hopkins is one that makes you feel like the stepping stones toward that goal are things that you are capable of reaching. Freshman year is a time of exploring your identity. There have been many times where I've wondered whether I belong at Hopkins, and perhaps it is in human nature to compare ourselves to others and compete. Hustle culture and impostor syndrome are rampant nowadays, especially as the world grows more advanced and there are increasingly more problems to solve. But every one of you freshmen deserve to be at Hopkins in one way or another. In a student body culture dominated by pre-meds and STEM majors, either fitting in or feeling unique are often struggles. Instead of questioning whether you belong here, spend your time considering how you belong here, and in what ways you can contribute. Lean into the things you are passionate about, no matter how minor or seemingly trivial. What can start as a small hobby or interest can become your greatest strength. As a senior, there still seems to be endless things to look for: your club merch hoodie, that one research paper template from sophomore year, a job for postgrad and maybe even the energy to do those dense readings for the week. Throughout your journey here (and my own), there will be times of struggle, when the tide suddenly swells or a rip current forms right under you. But there will also be good times to match: clear skies, a nice breeze and calm tides. Because there is so much change in freshman year, moments of uncertainty are all but inevitable. Learning how to float with its current, rather than against it, will lead to greater clarity when all you see are gray skies. And who knows, maybe the current will carry you to a place where you were always meant to find. Ayden Min is a senior majoring in International Studies from Los Angeles, Calif. She is a Managing Editor for The News-Letter.

articles.title: How I signed up for every club at Hopkins (and which ones you should join, too)
articles.description: With nearly 400 student organizations on campus, there is no shortage of clubs at Hopkins, but finding where you belong can be a daunting task. While the University organizes events like the iconic, semesterly Student Involvement Fair (SIF) or brings together a list of events occurring on campus through HopkinsGroups to help students connect with clubs, just knowing which organizations exist doesn't always mean you'll immediately find which clubs you fit in with. That's where I hope to shed some light. Like most freshmen, I used SIF as my opportunity to join every club I could think of. If it piqued my interest, my name was on the signup sheet. What I quickly realized, however, was how unfeasible my plan was. Within a week, my inbox was flooded with emails from clubs I barely even remembered, bombarding me with reminders to fill out the application forms. I never thought that club sign-ups could be that overwhelming, but now that I've gone through it, I can offer you some advice on how to avoid the stress of extracurricular sign ups. I've compiled a list of clubs that I stuck with throughout my freshman year, and I hope that they give you some guidance on how to approach your freshman fall. The Johns Hopkins News-Letter I wouldn't be much of a staff member if I didn't plug The News-Letter as my number-one recommendation for which clubs to join. I joined the staff during the beginning of my freshman fall as a Copy Editor, a position I've grown to love. While I didn't know any people on the editorial staff prior to joining, within a few weeks, I quickly grew to recognize my place. Whether it was through the various social events that the staff hosted or saying "hi" to familiar faces around campus, being on The News-Letter has been one of the highlights of my freshman year, and I encourage all new students who are interested in writing to give it a chance. Whether your interest lies in news, science or the arts, the various sections of the publication mean that everyone can explore their interests with us. Thread While technically not an on-campus organization, Thread is a great club to join if you want to break out of the Hopkins Bubble and get involved with the Baltimore community. The organization partners you with a high school student from Baltimore who needs a peer mentor, and you act as their "family member" for as long as they need. The club's requirements are minimal: interact with your young person once per week and meet with your "family" once a month. Through my time with Thread, I've formed a meaningful connection with my mentee, and by working with them, I've learned skills that I can take with me for the rest of my life, including navigating challenging scenarios. I joined Thread and found out how I fit in the club by attending an info session, which was something my friend suggested. Even though I had never met the people at the meeting before, I was greeted with such hospitality and kindness that I immediately knew that I would want to stick with the club. The leadership team at Thread makes everyone feel welcome, and the highly customizable nature of the club means that finding your place is effortless. SHARE The final club I stuck with in my freshman year is known as SHARE, which stands for "Supporting Hospitals Abroad with Resources and Equipment." SHARE is a low-commitment, high-impact organization that exposes students to the healthcare industry in a unique way. Students spend time sorting through expiring medical supplies in the Hopkins Hospital to donate them abroad for communities that are in need. The way I made SHARE enjoyable my freshman year is by going to the hospital with my friends and making it a social activity. We'll bring speakers to the sorting room and talk while we sort, making the hours fly by. Additionally, SHARE meets once per month for our general body meetings, where we learn about new medical devices and how to gain additional hospital exposure, like signing up for shadowing or connecting with physicians. Despite the low time commitment, it is also one of the most fun clubs you can get involved with. Those are just a few of the hundreds of clubs that you can join, and in my opinion, some of the best ones. Have fun finding your place on campus! Ayan Chaganthi is a sophomore from Atlanta, Ga. majoring in Molecular and Cellular Biology. He is a Copy Editor for The News-Letter .

articles.title: First strides at the Hopkins ice rink
articles.description: The surface of the ice rink glistened under the spotlights as sparkles of snow descended gently from the night sky. Students and Baltimoreans alike, regardless of their differences, united in this place for a common purpose - to simply have a good time with friends and family. As song and laughter permeated the rink, the warmth of hot chocolate melted its way into the soul, and skates carved into the ice the feeling of carefree joy. Winter at Hopkins began to feel a little less cold and lonely. But man, did my wrist hurt. Reflexively, I had thrown out my arms to break my fall and landed directly on my left wrist. The impact resonated up to the hands and fingers, carrying a tingling, numb pain as if from the repeated pecks of a flock of ferocious blue jays. There I sat, resigned on the ice, completely overwhelmed by the wild momentum that had sent me tumbling backwards in such unspectacular fashion. Between the discomfort and feeling of powerlessness, this was my "welcome to the Hopkins ice rink" moment. Allow me to share my story of ice skating as a complete newbie... Shortly after the start of the spring semester of my freshman year, a good friend of mine (let's call him S) told me about the Hopkins ice rink. As someone who had never ice skated before, yet was eager to give it a try, I made arrangements with him and another good friend (let's call him R) to go check it out on a Friday evening. Fortunately for my inexperienced self, R and S had both skated before and were willing to show me the ropes. After arriving and putting on the skates, a sort of muted orange color with flattened blades for safety, it was time to set foot on the ice - or so I thought. I actually needed to get used to walking with skates normally first. Ok, now we're ready. As my blades came in contact with the ice, it felt as if I had entered a different dimension, drifting in a space where friction had left the chat, where every minute movement could snowball into a frantic avalanche. "Hold on to the rails and go slowly," R advised me. "Keep your center of gravity low and bend your knees." And so I made my first lap around the rink at a snail's pace, and then I completed another. Around me, I observed a variety of skill levels. Some glided effortlessly like R, others navigated with steady confidence like S and a few trudged cautiously by the rails just like me. With the guidance of my friends, as well as a skating aid in the form of a blue seal, I ventured an arm's length away from the safety of the rails and closer to the uncertainty of the center. Several shaky laps later, I had mustered the courage to trust my own balance. R suggested putting my hands on my knees, ensuring that my center of gravity stayed low and my balance remained stable. To turn at the corners of the rink, I needed to angle my feet and let my momentum carry me naturally. I practiced, slow and steady, and gradually increased my speed. At some point, I got ahead of myself, as I tend to do, and the rest is as you already know - ouch. When I went down with a thud, a pestering thought entered my mind that maybe I should give up on skating - maybe I'm just not cut out for it. But after a moment, I pushed it aside and reminded myself that I was just getting started. Not to mention, I was having a ton of fun. R and S came over, offered a hand and helped me up. And so I continued skating, no matter how ungracefully, with the lingering pain in my wrist as a reminder to stick to the fundamentals. The three of us returned every week until the rink shut down for the year, and I could feel myself improving each time through a growing collection of battles with lost balance. Somewhere along the way, I realized that my experience on the ice mirrored much of what it means to be a student at Hopkins. Let's be real here. Hopkins is tough. There are moments when you feel like you've finally found your groove, only to realize that the next midterm, project or paper is already looming over the horizon. Hopkins is competitive. It's easy to feel left behind when it seems that everyone else is perpetually on the grind to build their resumes, progress in their research and seek out internships, on top of excelling academically. But, like skating, what looks effortless from the outside is usually built on a lot of stumbling and recovery, and it's rarely done alone. Hopkins is the flock where real, unshakeable bonds are built. In between the stress and the constant motion, you find people who are going through it with you, and that shared connection becomes something special. Much like on the ice rink, it's through a cycle of stumbles, adjustments and getting back up again that you grow - one stride at a time. Andrew Wu is a sophomore majoring in Biomedical Engineering from Northville, Mich. and is a Cartoons Editor for The News-Letter .

articles.title: A beginner's guide to being an international student at Hopkins
articles.description: Welcome to what may become four of the most memorable years of your life! Jokes aside, my time at Hopkins has been one of the most memorable and life-changing experiences of my life so far. As an international student, this experience can look a little different for us than it does for domestic students. Personally, I moved from Melbourne, Australia, which is just about as far as you can possibly go, and it wasn't always easy. Thankfully, technology has made distance a lot easier, and so have the people around me. You will probably go through moments when you miss your friends back home, when you wish you could have one more home-cooked meal or when you just can't understand why there's no decent public transport network in Baltimore! I can't guarantee it will always feel worth it, but by embracing everything with an open mind, you can make this new city feel like a new home. So, without further ado, let's get into some of the basics that will help you make the most of your time at Hopkins! Get involved on campus Moving away from home poses many challenges, but perhaps the biggest is leaving your loved ones behind and starting over in a new country. It can be incredibly daunting to put yourself out there with a whole bunch of people you've never met, but it is that same vulnerability that can help you meet people who share a similar outlook on life. Whether it's saying hello to someone in your class or striking up a conversation about a shared interest, you never know who you might meet! Joining a club on campus can be one of the best ways to find people with similar interests. For me, writing about sports was something I had never had the chance to do. When I arrived at Hopkins, I took a step forward and discovered something I enjoyed that introduced me to a whole group of people I wouldn't have otherwise met. Keep an eye out for the Student Involvement Fair, which is one of the best ways to familiarize yourself with all of the groups on campus. Simply taking that step to get involved can be so rewarding and is one of the easiest (and most fun) ways to get more acclimated to your new surroundings at college! Additionally, familiarizing yourself with resources like the Office of International Services (OIS) and student groups such as International Students at Hopkins (ISAH) can help you to find answers to questions you might have during your time here. The OIS can be particularly helpful with queries about visas and work authorization, while ISAH offers access to valuable resources such as grocery runs or city excursions where you can meet and connect with other international students. Explore the city While I'm sure you've heard all about how great Washington, D.C. and New York City are, it's important that you also explore all the amazing things Baltimore has to offer! For those who enjoy spending time exploring the arts, I cannot recommend the Walters Art Museum enough. Admission is completely free, and the Walters has displays ranging from ancient Egyptian and Chinese art to French impressionism and everything in between! A particular favorite of mine is the room of Ancient Roman sarcophagi with intricate designs carved into their exteriors that tell various stories from Bacchanalian mythology. The Baltimore Museum of Art is also worth a visit, with plenty of incredible exhibits ranging from ancient works to modern and post-modern art. Alternatively, Baltimore is a city with a rich sports culture, and I tell everyone that they should go to at least one Orioles game while they are here. Sports are such an integral part of American culture, and what is more American than a hot dog and a baseball game? Watch out for student discount nights when you can get tickets for just $10! We are also lucky to have access to all kinds of cuisines and amazing cafés, so you'll never run out of options. Some personal favorites of mine include The Helmand for Afghan food, Chiapparelli's Restaurant (I would come here just for the starter salad and bread) and Blue Moon Cafe for a brunch that will fill you up for the whole day. And, of course, you have to try some American favorites like Chipotle, Popeyes or Taco Bell! Finally, just taking a walk around Baltimore can be the perfect way to spend an afternoon. I would highly recommend taking a stroll around Fells Point or up to Federal Hill for some incredible views of the city. This is just a snapshot of the possibilities in Baltimore, so I encourage you to go out and explore for yourself. We are very lucky to be in such proximity to all the other East Coast cities, and you should go and see them, but just remember that there is so much to do in Baltimore as well! Take time for yourself I want to emphasize that it is completely normal not to always feel comfortable. You have taken an enormous step in moving to a new place to study, and that in and of itself is a testament to your bravery and courage. Don't be afraid to let yourself think about the things you miss, the people you wish you could be around and the good memories you have back home. This experience is just as much about learning about yourself as it is about learning about your intro biology class. When things get stressful (which they probably will), it's okay to turn to your basics, whether that's going on a walk, watching a movie with friends or trying a new bakery. We are also incredibly lucky to have access to a wealth of free mental health resources at Hopkins, all of which are there to support you through this journey that you are undertaking. Never tell yourself that any issue is too small, because there is always someone there who wants to help you succeed in every facet of your life. Enjoy yourself! My final message is simple: enjoy yourself. We are all fortunate to be at this institution, but there is no single right way to experience Hopkins. Some days will be exciting and others may be overwhelming, but the most important thing is to make sure you enjoy this time in whatever manner best suits you. Good luck, and remember to bring a warm coat, because winters can get cold! Freddy Branson is a senior majoring in Classical Flute Performance from Melbourne, Australia. He is a Sports Editor for The News-Letter.

articles.title: A handy starter kit for touring charm city
articles.description: Welcome, new Blue Jays! As you start getting used to your new nest, I suggest keeping an open mind. There's a lot to do in the city if you're willing to spread your wings - whether through the public transport circulators, the JHMI shuttles or good old fashioned walking. Here are some highlights of Charm City to get you started! An assortment of essentials These are some names you'll see constantly circulated in the coming weeks. Inner Harbor features several historic ships (I recommend the Ghost tour!). Just a walk away is Fells Point, with some of Baltimore's best eateries, including every student's favorite: Ekiben. Each location also features a special treat for tea lovers; try out Cuples Tea House and The Spice & Tea Exchange. Along the JHMI route, Station North is home to several artsy sites and theaters including the Charles Theater, the Baltimore Jewelry Center, the True Vine Record Shop and the Stavros Niarchos Foundation (SNF) Parkway. Peabody and the surrounding Mount Vernon area are also almost always buzzing with events to check out. An assortment of greenery When you want to leave behind the red bricks of the Hopkins campus, Baltimore has some green patches waiting. Sherwood Gardens and the Guilford Reservoir are small areas near Homewood Campus worth spending some time in. Also nearby, Stony Run Trail is an excellent site to go birding. A fair walk away, you can reconnect with nature at the Cylburn Arboretum, Rawlings Conservatory and the Maryland Zoo. If you walk the other way, Lake Montebello is not a bad hang-out spot, and Patterson Park near the medical campus is a classic space to indulge in fresh air (although the observatory is currently closed). An assortment of graveyards Let's veer away from all that talk of leafy life to spotlight Baltimore's most talented headstones. The famed writer Edgar Allan Poe, buried at Westminster Hall, can be found only a short walk from the Peabody campus. At Green Mount Cemetery, you can visit famous assassin John Wilkes Booth, 'Freaks' actor Johnny Eck and the little known historical figure Johns Hopkins (ever heard of him?). For those willing to take a longer walk, the famed drag queen Divine is buried in Towson. Halloween plans galore! An assortment of museums Baltimore is home to several museums worth your time. Don't ignore the on-campus museums, including the Gilman Archaeological Museum and Homewood Museum which display key historical artifacts and have a rich connection to the school's history. The nearby Baltimore Museum of Art also features an assortment of art pieces from across time periods and cultures. Towards Peabody campus, take a trip to the similarly expansive Walters Art Museum and the Maryland Center of History and Culture, which takes a deeper look at various sociopolitical artifacts relevant to the state's history. The National Great Blacks in Wax Museum also presents a truly unique collection. If you go onwards to the Inner Harbor area, you'll find several more museums including the fascinatingly eclectic American Visionary Art Museum, the Baltimore Museum of Industry and the Reginald F. Lewis Museum which spotlights Black history. A walk away, you can find museums dedicated to key historical figures such as baseball player Babe Ruth and journalist H. L. Mencken. Some distance from there, the National Museum of Railroad History & Innovation features a historic locomotive collection. An assortment of history With every other building being 200 years old, Baltimore has quite a few important pieces of history under its belt. Most famously, the national anthem of the United States was written at the historic Fort McHenry, which remains a lovely tourist destination today. Other key Baltimore firsts include the United States' first public gas street lamp right outside the Peale, the first purpose-built museum in the nation. The Baltimore Basilica also marks the first cathedral in the country. If you get tired of visiting all these locations, you can refill your supplies at the Lexington Market - which is America's oldest continuously running public market. An assortment of events While exploring these locations, don't forget to engage with some classic events around the city. Artscape marks Baltimore's biggest annual festival for the arts. Other annual celebrations, typically during the May-June period, include a Flower Mart, a Kinetic Sculpture Race and the Fells Point Fun Festival. More regularly, First Thursdays at Canton Waterfront Park feature free concerts. Bibliophiles will also enjoy the Book Thing of Baltimore near campus, where you can pick from an assortment of free used books. Pick your categories, mix-and-match or fly well beyond the options listed here. Happy adventuring! Aditya Sankar is a sophomore majoring in Molecular and Cellular Biology and Behavioral Biology from Bangalore, India. He is a Science and Technology Editor for The News-Letter .

articles.title: Baltimore's must-visit movie theatre: The Charles
articles.description: One of my favorite Hopkins experiences spawned outside campus confines. Inside The Charles Theatre , I was seated for a revival screening of Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey . Kubrick's unsettling sci-fi film moves unexpectedly through its depiction of space and humanity, but I had seen it before. I knew what to expect. I had been to this theatre before to watch old and new films in this exact auditorium, and I would keep to myself until the end of its runtime. But at this instance, Natalie Wang, an English and Film major from the Class of 2026, sat in the same row as me. She recognized me from the one class we shared, and we initially made fine but mundane conversation. As a foundation for our conversation, I had a background knowledge of film, including the one we were about to see. But what moved our discussion beyond basic pleasantries was the theatre we were in. I half-jokingly stated that if I was not at Hopkins I was here, and she replied similarly. We bonded over the movies we saw in this theatre, and she explained that some of her film classes hosted screenings here too. She would invite me to some of those screenings, and we would go to several more movies together in between the coursework we got through. The movie theatre gives more than spontaneous friendships. Like new relationships, movies convey an experience outside yourself. There's a bit of escapism in seeing someone else live a life, and a bit of voyeurism seeing someone else's suffering. It's honestly a crude experience when you dissect it. But when you watch a movie at home, you're prone to distractions, and then you're no longer looking at the picture at all. Or the picture is wrong; the image is distorted on your phone, laptop or dorm-compliant-too-small television. The stripped viewing experience brings none of the satisfaction that a theatrical screening does. The Charles, Baltimore's oldest theatre from 1939 , has massively enriched my life with its screenings. Whenever I'm feeling too stressed from Hopkins, I take the JHMI shuttle to the Penn Station stop and take a five-minute walk to The Charles. Located in the Station North Arts and Entertainment District, The Charles can't be missed; it's a beautiful Beaux-Arts building designed as a streetcar. The theater's offerings are vast and affordable. Prices are tax-free and, with a student ID, tickets are $12 . The Charles shows a variety of independent and foreign films along with major studio prestige pictures. Its revival series , where the theatre presents repository films, is how I saw 2001: A Space Odyssey . Through its revival series, I've seen works by David Cronenberg, Alfred Hitchcock, and David Lynch on the big screen. At home, you can rewatch an old movie endlessly, but seeing it in the cinema is incomparable. I've enjoyed seeing new, small releases in the theatre too. I've cherished the accompanying experiences in doing so, such as talking to an older Hungarian woman about Sophy Romvari's Blue Heron and how "it certainly wasn't an American movie." Talking with others about a movie has always provided humor or insight or both. The solitary viewing experience at home feels lackluster in comparison. The theatrical experience, simultaneously individual and social and grounding and dream-like, is the best at independent theaters where the goal is showing great films. While you're a student, visit The Charles, and maybe you'll see something new, talk to a stranger or get some reprieve from your life for a bit. River Phan is a juniormajoring in English from Silver Spring, Md. and is an Arts & Entertainment Editor for The News-Letter .

articles.title: On the college experience: Making friends looks different for everyone
articles.description: After helping me move all my stuff into the first floor of Griffin house, my parents dropped me off right outside AMR II. I hugged them once, tightly, and walked through the security gates. Then I unlocked my dorm door and started unpacking my clothes. I felt fine -a little dazed from so many changes at once, yes, but I wasn't crying. That night, my roommate and I walked to Homewood Field, where I found First-Year Mentor (FYM) Group 75 sitting in a circle. I remember sitting there, shaking hands with the first few people I met as an undergraduate, listening to orientation leaders welcome me to Hopkins. I thought about the thousands of people around me, a whole class of people I'd be living with for the next four years, none of whom I knew. All the people I did know were at least a hundred miles away. Not that far, I know -I'm only from New Jersey -but it still felt massive. Even then, I felt alright. I figured out how to use the communal shower, set my alarm and went to sleep. It was somewhere in the middle of the second day that it hit me: a sense of isolation and homesickness. After showing up late to my first FYM group meeting with a cup of half-finished decaf coffee (the only thing available in Hopkins Cafe) and an incoming migraine from the lack of caffeine, I watched the other members of my group form friendships in the first few days. Though I smiled and walked with the group and held conversations about names, majors and hometowns with people I met at Hopkins Cafe, I didn't see myself forming all the relationships I thought I was supposed to be forming. I felt lost. I wasn't great at small talk, and, most importantly, I didn't know how to make friends. I'd met my high school friends by chance; I hadn't tried to make them. Fall semester passed quickly, and the sense of isolation persisted. Birthdays passed. I called my family and high school friends often. Most of my time was spent in the library. I'd made some friends -people I got lunch and dinner with, someone from my FYM group who would eventually become my roommate for the next three years - but I felt that I was missing out on what most people had already: a "college experience." I was told it meant staying up until 4 a.m. with friends, partying late, getting drunk, having weekends filled with plans. This, I didn't have. At Hopkins, my friends took time. I met two of my close friends freshman year, two of my close friends sophomore year and a whole bunch of friends junior year. The canonical "college experience" too, took time, and it didn't take the forms I'd expected. Sophomore year, I stayed up until four talking with a friend I'd met by chance after asking him to review a poem I'd written. I also went to my first party that year, a Halloween party which I didn't like as much as I thought I would. Junior year, I went on my first spring break trip with my friends, a week-long trip to Montréal. These experiences weren't what I'd envisioned in my freshman year, and they weren't the relationships I'd seen others making in that first week of orientation. They were mine - experiences that I liked, friends that I connected with, in my own way. Over the last three years, I learned that my favorite things to do with friends were bake pumpkin pies in their houses and play Settlers of Catan until 12 a.m. For you, they might look different. There's no right answer -and looking at others to figure out how you're supposed to be living might be the wrong answer. So for any incoming or current student who might feel isolated in college relative to their peers, just remember: college looks different for everyone. And if your college experiences take a little more time, or you feel out of place, I ask you to trust yourself. You're not alone. Lana Swindle is a senior majoring in Philosophy and Writing Seminars from Princeton, N.J. She is a Copy Editor for The News-Letter.

articles.title: The mug I never returned
articles.description: In the nonstop tornado that defines life at Hopkins, stress quickly becomes part of our everyday routine. It all starts from the very beginning of freshman year, making it hard to consistently set time aside for our mental health. Syllabus week does not exist at Hopkins. Instead, it is syllabus "ten minutes," where, in a matter of moments, every freshman is thrust under a mountain of assignments and expected to navigate what is quite literally a whole new universe independently. For me, at least at first, the transition from high school's structured environment to Hopkins' sink-or-swim mentality felt like a breath of fresh air. Pretty soon though, it hit me like a tsunami. When I first arrived at the chaos, I wasn't sure how to deal with it. I missed the small comforting routines I had at home: waking up to my Disney princess alarm clock at 6:15 a.m., being able to put mozzarella sticks in the air fryer whenever I wanted and my dog darting toward me whenever I walked through the front door. At college, something as simple as making a good cup of coffee suddenly feels impossible when you're trying to create an Introductory Chemistry Quizlet with one hand while trying not to forget to grab your laundry in exactly nine minutes. Otherwise, someone will dump out your clothes, and you can kiss your last matching pairs of socks goodbye. This constant rush overwhelmed me. I realized that this way of living simply wasn't sustainable. I needed to find a way to pause. It was in that search for stillness that I found my anchor: a plain white dining hall mug that I accidentally carried out of FFC during my second week on campus. It started out as an absent-minded mistake. I was walking out with my coffee still in hand while rushing to my 9 a.m. lecture. Since then, though, it has become an unexpected blessing. My mug is more than just a vessel for drinks. I've used it as a pencil holder during late-night study sessions, a container for hair ties on my dresser, a spoon stand while eating Lucky Charms in my dorm and even as a temporary herb garden for the random mint plant I found at the 32nd Street Farmers Market. Most importantly, though, my mug holds the coffee that starts each day. Making coffee in it has become my morning ritual. I carefully fill it with hot water from my electric kettle and measure out the coffee granules, creamer and sugar. I'll admit my coffee combinations are a hit or miss, but I value the agency I have over creating them. During those few minutes, I'm not a student worrying about my GPA or a freshman trying to find friends. I'm just a person enjoying the rich aroma of Nescafé and the warmth lingering on my fingertips. This ritual forces me to slow down, become aware of the present moment and breathe before stepping into another day at Hopkins. My mug doesn't make Hopkins any less demanding, nor does it magically reduce my workload. What it gives me is five uninterrupted minutes every morning that belong entirely to me. Once I realized how much those five minutes mattered, I started noticing that everyone around me seemed to have their own version of a mug: their own ritual that made Hopkins feel just a little more manageable. Every undergraduate here faces similar pressures: jargon-filled exams where you need a dictionary just to understand the questions, endless tasks that pile up faster than we can complete them and expectations to excel with ease in one of the nation's most rigorous academic environments. We all search for ways to make college feel less overwhelming. We all seek our own anchors in the tornado. For my friend Leah, it's her afternoon journaling near Mudd Hall after her classes. She says the feeling of putting pen to paper after being stressed all day is what she looks forward to. For my friend Sophie, it's eating takeout from Lao Sze Chuan every Saturday. She says the taste of food that isn't Hopkins affiliated allows her to decompress and reenergize. These rituals, though, extend beyond individual practices. I've noticed how groups of students form their own anchoring traditions: the AMR II students who dress up and go out every Friday night, matcha lovers making their way to KANOM Cafe, and acapella groups gathering in the Bloomberg Student Center to sing their favorite tunes. These are rituals that have become their anchors. They don't make Hopkins any less demanding, but they remind us that even in the middle of the tornado, we can choose moments that bring us back to ourselves. Practicing mental health as a freshman isn't some niche idea, even though it's often treated that way. A quick Google search will tell you that "good" mental health means consistent sleep (7-9 hours), a nutritious diet and regular exercise. But let's be honest - that's not realistic for most freshmen at Hopkins. Many of us rely on Hopkins Cafe for most of our meals, our sleep gets squeezed by coursework and other commitments and, personally, I used to live two minutes away from the Ralph S. O'Connor Recreation Center and went a grand total of three times this year, all during the first week of school. What actually matters is this: taking care of your mental health as a freshman means deciding to set aside time for yourself, not feeling guilty about it and recognizing that it doesn't have to be big or perfect. Sometimes, it's as simple as a cup of coffee in a plain white dining hall mug. It won't make your exams easier or your workload lighter, but it can remind you that before you're a Hopkins student, you're a person. Rhea Makkuni is a sophomore from Chicago, Ill. majoring in Molecular and Cellular Biology. She is a Science & Technology Editor for The News-Letter .

articles.title: Dry Martian Meteorite Reveals Early Water in Mars's Crust
articles.description: Billions of years ago, Mars was hypothesized to have been a habitable world with flowing liquid water and the potential for life. But directly studying its ancient past is currently limited to orbiters and rovers, as scientists have yet to obtain direct samples from Mars. However, meteorites have been found on Earth to have potentially originated from Mars during large impacts that flung chunks of the Red Planet into space, eventually being grabbed by Earth’s gravity and crashing into the Earth’s surface.

articles.title: Reading Thucydides in the wolf world
articles.description: The term Thucydides’s Trap has caught on since Professor Graham Allison wrote his 2017 book, Destined for War: Can America and China Escape Thucydides’s Trap? The core concept comes from Greek soldier-historian Thucydides’s History of the Peloponnesian War who identifies the structural stress that occurs when a major rising power is perceived to threaten to displace an established power. My intention here is not to explain Allison’s work or his treatment of the trap but to point to how modern-day scholars and policymakers cherrypick episodes from Thucydides’s work to justify their own approaches. I believe, as the post-World War II international security architecture unravels and we enter what some describe as the wolf world, that it is important to analyse Thucydides’s history in view of the book’s hermeneutics rather than picking up episodes that suit one’s own predilections. Thucydides arrived in the United States policy corridors with Dr Henry Kissinger. He had taught the text at Harvard and was keenly familiar with it. But upon joining Richard Nixon’s administration in the White House, he sought fit to focus on the Melian Dialogue, colouring outside the lines. The one line, “The strong exact what they can; the weak concede what they must,” became the slogan of Cold War strategies. Kissinger knew that Thucydides message was far more nuanced and he was not justifying imperial overreach. But that was for the classroom. The world Kissinger had to tackle was one in which ‘man was wolf to man,’ homo homini lupus of Plautus popularised by Thomas Hobbes. That misrepresentation has generally informed US policymakers since then. Now that cruder minds are ruling America and the precepts of International Law, for whatever they were worth, have been defenestrated and America’s foreign policy has become a Kabuki theatre, a few words about Thucydides’s work are in order. The structural architecture of History of the Peloponnesian War relies on a psychological arc that connects the Plague of Athens, the Melian Dialogue (nearly 14 years later) and the Sicilian Expedition (a year later). Far from putting down a simple chronicle of military manoeuvres, Thucydides tracks the internal rot of the Athenian psyche through the description of the Plague. By tracing this trajectory, the reader discovers that the moral dissolution initiated by the plague directly fostered the intellectual hubris that were to lead to Melos, which inevitably culminated in the material ruin of the Sicilian campaign. The foundational fracture occurs in Book Two with the Plague (430 BCE). Thucydides describes a city where the sudden, indiscriminate terror of death obliterates law ( nomos ) and religious restraint. Faced with immediate mortality, citizens abandon honour for instant gratification, arguing that the virtuous and the wicked die alike. This lawlessness ( anomia ) institutionalises a new societal ethos: the abandonment of traditional justice in favour of self-interest and survival. The plague does not merely kill bodies; it extinguishes the moral constraints of the polis. Might and appetite replace civic virtue. The plague, Thucydides tells us, also claimed Pericles and his family. That death, within the hermeneutics of the text, becomes a metaphor for the demise of nomos. The emergence of more populist and aggressive figures, such as Cleon, who prioritised personal popularity and raw emotion over steady strategy, comes to symbolise anomia. This internalised lawlessness manifests later as aggressive foreign policy in the Melian Dialogue (416 BCE) of Book Five. But the seeds of Melos were sown earlier. Two years after Pericles’ death, Athens had the Mytilenian debate between Cleon and Diodotus. Cleon fiercely argued in favour of executing the entire population of Mytilene to send a message of terror. While Diodotus narrowly persuaded the assembly to reverse the decision to execute all citizens, the Athenians still exacted a brutal and bloody punishment on the city. At Melos, the Athenian envoys articulate a chilling political realism, famously declaring that, “the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.” This worldview seems to be the direct philosophical descendant of the plague’s nihilism. Having lost their respect for divine law and cosmic justice during the pestilence, the Athenians now claim that the rule of the stronger is a universal law of nature. The moral decay hardened into intellectual hubris. Athens no longer seeks to justify its empire through justice or leadership, but purely through raw, unyielding power. The immediate narrative pivot to the Sicilian Expedition (415–413 BCE) in Book Six reveals this hubris in action, dramatised through the opposing speeches of Nicias and Alcibiades. Nicias represents the ghost of old Athenian moderation. He desperately warns the assembly against overreach, cautioning that they are leaving enemies behind to chase a massive, unknown island. But the plague-damaged psyche of Athens, now driven entirely by imperial appetite and the illusion of invincibility, cannot tolerate restraint. Instead, they rally behind Alcibiades (notice the shift from the Cleon-Diodotus debate). Alcibiades is brilliant, reckless, and entirely devoid of civic responsibility. He appeals to the city’s insatiable desire for expansion, arguing that an empire must grow or it will wither. Ultimately, Thucydides’s narrative acts as a tragic warning. The lawlessness born in the plague pits became the strategic blindness that was to mock the Melians and finally drove Athens to sail into the Sicilian trap. In Sicily, the inversion is completed. The Athenians are utterly destroyed, reduced to the same desperate reliance on “hope” and suffering that they had ridiculed at Melos. Through this connection Thucydides demonstrates that the real danger of power overreach is not always external opposition but the internal erosion of the moral and intellectual clarity required to understand the limits of power. There are no perfect analogies but history’s verdicts are often uncannily similar. The writer has an abiding interest in foreign and security policies and life’s ironies. articles.title: Albert Codinas
articles.description: Cervantes, Colón, Da Vinci, Shakespeare, Hernán Cortés... y ahora, Juana la Loca. El Institut Nova Història (INH) no descansa en su empeño por convertir la historiografía en ficción. Su última "contribución" ha sido presentar una tesis que sostiene que la monarca no nació en Toledo, sino en Cardona, bajo el argumento de que España borró su rastro catalán.

articles.title: Queen bees have a disturbing way to survive pesticides
articles.description: Honeybee queens exposed to pesticides can shift some of the contamination into their eggs, revealing a previously unknown survival strategy. The process may protect the queen while putting developing offspring, and potentially the entire colony, at risk.
